notes: AG reference on unduly lenient robbery sentences; aggravating features and sentencing bracket analysis are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Unduly lenient sentences for robbery of vulnerable man at home
key_facts: Randall and Donaghue pleaded guilty to robbing a frail 57-year-old man with learning difficulties at his home at night, using gratuitous violence and stealing about £100 in savings.
The victim suffered facial fractures; three offenders were involved and Randall later breached bail.
At Gloucester Crown Court each offender received three years' imprisonment for robbery, with Randall receiving an additional four months consecutive for failing to surrender.
The Attorney General referred the sentences as unduly lenient given the targeting of a vulnerable victim, home invasion, group attack, and significant injury.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 concerning unduly lenient Crown Court sentences.
enrichment.outcome: Reference allowed; three-year robbery sentences set aside and replaced with five and a half years' imprisonment in each case, allowing for double jeopardy (Randall's total including bail offence: five years ten months).
enrichment.ratio: Robberies involving gratuitous violence against a known vulnerable victim in his own home at night, causing significant injury and involving a group, warrant sentences in the range of about six and a half to seven years before double jeopardy on a guilty plea; three years was unduly lenient and insufficiently deterrent.
legal_issues: Whether three-year sentences for this home robbery were unduly lenient
The appropriate sentencing bracket for robbery of elderly or vulnerable victims at home
How much weight to give guilty pleas, remorse, and absence of surgical treatment
Whether initial non-robbery intent or vigilante motive reduced culpability
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference Nos 32 and 33 of 1995 (Pegg and Martin) [1996] 2 Cr App R (S) 346
Attorney General's Reference No 89 of 1999 (Farrow) [2000] 2 Cr App R (S) 382
Attorney General's Reference 48 of 2000 (Johnson) [2001] 1 Cr App R (S) 423

notes: Asylum and Article 3 appeal from DRC; adjudicator reasoning and discrepancy with brother's case are well documented.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum appeal where political motive for family attack not proved
key_facts: Mr Otshudi claimed asylum after Congolese troops attacked his family in Mbuji-Mayi in August 2002, killing his mother, raping family members, and abducting his father.
The adjudicator found the account credible but was not satisfied to the low standard required that the attack was motivated by the father's low-level UDPS political support.
She also rejected the Article 3 claim on the basis that the attack was an isolated incident and no objective risk of repetition was shown on return.
Eleven days after the IAT dismissed this appeal, a different adjudicator allowed the brother's claim on essentially the same evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission of Kay LJ against the Immigration Appeal Tribunal's dismissal of an asylum and human rights appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator may reject an asylum claim where, even accepting the attack occurred, the applicant fails to show even modest proof of a Convention reason such as political opinion; absence of an alternative explanation does not require the decision-maker to speculate, and a divergent outcome in a linked sibling case does not itself establish legal error.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator erred in rejecting a political motive without weighing alternative explanations
Whether the IAT adequately addressed the Article 3 risk-of-return claim
Whether inconsistent adjudicator decisions on identical evidence provide a ground of challenge
The proper approach to fact-finding review after Subesh and Karanakaran
linked_authorities: Subesh [2004] EWCA Civ 56
Indrakumar [2003] EWCA Civ 1677
Karanakaran (25 January 2000)
Ravichandran [1996] Imm AR 97

confidence.notes: Core asylum and Article 3 reasoning is detailed. The postscript on the brother's case is obiter and humanitarian rather than dispositive.

notes: Children relocation appeal; Payne v Payne discipline and retrial disposal are clearly explained.

enrichment.short_title: Child relocation to Australia: flawed welfare assessment requires retrial
key_facts: A mother sought to relocate two young daughters from England to Adelaide after remarrying an Australian resident; contact with the father had previously been agreed and complied with.
County court proceedings lasted about eighteen months with flawed CAFCASS reporting and delayed trial before HHJ Douse refused relocation in January 2004.
The judge gave extensive reasons but failed adequately to assess the emotional impact on the mother of refusing relocation, contrary to the Payne v Payne discipline.
The court rejected a proposed new 'lifestyle choice' sub-category of relocation cases.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission treated as full hearing against refusal of a mother's application to remove children from the jurisdiction to Australia.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted for retrial before a specialist family judge; no order for costs.
enrichment.ratio: In leave-to-remove cases the trial judge must fully assess the consequence to the primary carer of refusing a realistic relocation proposal and weigh that against detriment to the child from lost contact; failure to do so is a material error even where the outcome is finely balanced, and retrial rather than substitution is the principled disposal where adverse findings were made on oral evidence.
legal_issues: Whether the judge adequately applied Payne v Payne paragraph 40(c) on impact of refusal on the mother
Whether criticism of the mother for not offering additional contact was lawful
Whether relocation cases involving lifestyle choice require a distinct legal approach
Whether the Court of Appeal should substitute its own welfare decision or order retrial
linked_authorities: Payne v Payne [2001] 1 FLR 1052
Re B; Re S (Removal from the Jurisdiction) [2003] 2 FLR 1043
Lonslow v Hennig [1986] 2 FLR 378
Poel v Poel [1970] 1 WLR 1469

confidence.notes: Error of principle and retrial disposal are explicit. Detailed factual welfare balance at retrial remains undecided.

notes: Major Jamaica Article 3 certification appeal; sufficiency of state protection analysis is detailed and authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: Jamaica section 94 certification quashed for perceived informer risk
key_facts: A Jamaican visitor overstayer claimed asylum alleging persecution as a perceived PNP informer and as a perceived homosexual after JLP-linked violence in a garrison area.
The Secretary of State rejected the claims and certified them as clearly unfounded under section 94, removing in-country appeal rights.
Expert evidence from Mr Hilaire Sobers challenged whether Jamaica could protect informers or perceived informers from gang reprisals, including after relocation.
A deputy High Court judge upheld certification, but fresh Sobers reports were admitted on appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission of Laws LJ against refusal of judicial review of clearly unfounded certification under section 94 of the 2002 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; certification quashed; appellant entitled to in-country appeal to an adjudicator on the merits.
enrichment.ratio: Section 94 certification requires that no legitimate view of the evidence could allow the claim to succeed; where credible expert and country material raises a serious question whether Jamaica provides reasonable practical protection against Article 3 ill-treatment for informers or perceived informers, and internal relocation is also genuinely in issue, certification is unlawful even if the claimant may ultimately fail on appeal.
legal_issues: The meaning and application of the clearly unfounded certification test
Whether Jamaica provides sufficiency of state protection for informers and perceived informers
Whether internal relocation within Jamaica was a viable answer to the Article 3 claim
The symmetry of approach between refugee Convention and Article 3 non-state actor cases

Horvath v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] 1 AC 489
A v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 175
R (L) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] 1 All ER 1062
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex p Thangarasa; ex p Yogathas [2002] 3 WLR 1276

notes: Retained firefighters test case; split outcome on Reg 2(3)(f) construction versus similar-work comparison is clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Retained firefighters and part-time worker comparability under Reg 2

statutes_considered.title: Part-Time Workers (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2000

key_facts: Representative retained firefighters claimed less favourable treatment than whole-time colleagues in pensions, responsibility pay, and sick pay.
The employment tribunal dismissed the claims, finding different contract types under Regulation 2(3)(f) and that the roles were not the same or broadly similar work.
The Employment Appeal Tribunal upheld both grounds.
The Court of Appeal held retained firefighters fell within Regulation 2(3)(a), not the residual category (f), but upheld the tribunal on similar-work comparability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal in a test case concerning national retained firefighter terms and conditions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Court of Appeal reversed the tribunals on contract-type construction but affirmed dismissal on the similar-work issue; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 2(3)(f) is a residual category for workers outside paragraphs (a) to (e), not a route for employers to remove otherwise comparable part-time employees from protection by reasonableness; however, where whole-time firefighters perform measurable additional non-emergency functions requiring higher qualifications and skills, a tribunal may lawfully find they are not engaged in the same or broadly similar work as retained firefighters.
legal_issues: Whether retained and whole-time firefighters are employed under the same type of contract for Regulation 2(4)
The proper construction of Regulation 2(3)(f)
Whether the roles involve the same or broadly similar work
Whether the tribunal erred by focusing on recruitment, promotion, and ancillary duties

Yeboah v Crofton [2002] EWCA Civ 794
Montgomery v Johnson Underwood Ltd [2001] EWCA Civ 318

notes: Complex nine-issue cruise insurance appeal after 9/11; most issues dismissed but issue (iii) allowed; full claim outcome depends on remitted quantification.

enrichment.short_title: Silversea 9/11 loss-of-income insurance policy construction appeal
key_facts: Silversea claimed under a fleet loss-of-income policy after passenger bookings fell following the 11 September 2001 attacks and subsequent travel warnings.

Cover Ai insured loss due to listed perils including terrorism and acts of war or armed conflict interfering with scheduled itineraries; cover Aii insured market losses from war, armed conflict, or terrorism.
The underwriters denied much of the claim on limits, timing, policy structure, and causation grounds; Tomlinson J largely found for the underwriters.
The appeal raised nine issues on policy construction, including whether 9/11 was acts of war or armed conflict.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a Commercial Court judgment on construction and quantification of a cruise fleet loss-of-income insurance claim arising from 9/11.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs, save that issue (iii) on the six-month measurement period under cover Aii was allowed in Silversea's favour.
enrichment.ratio: Under this policy, market-based booking losses belong principally under cover Aii rather than cover Ai, which requires loss of time and interference with scheduled itineraries; the Aii aggregate limit is fleet-wide at $5 million; the six-month Aii period measures fall-off across the marketed cruise programme rather than defining only sailings commencing within six months.
legal_issues: Whether the cover Aii limit is $5 million per vessel or fleet-wide
Whether rectification could convert the Aii limit to a fleet cap
How the six-month Aii measurement period operates
Whether booking losses fall within cover Ai or only cover Aii
Whether 9/11 constituted acts of war or armed conflict under the policy
linked_authorities: Kawasaki Kisen Kabushiki Kaisha of Kobe v Bantham Steamship Company Limited [1939] 2 KB 544
Spinneys (1948) Ltd v Royal Insurance Co Ltd [1980] 1 Lloyd's Rep 406

confidence.notes: Nine separate issues and partial success make summary enrichment harder. Issue (ix) on war/armed conflict was argued but not finally decided dispositively.

notes: GMC judicial review after criminal acquittals; Rule 11(2) and Redgrave principles are carefully analysed.

enrichment.short_title: GMC may refer acquitted indecent assault cases under Rule 11(2)

statutes_considered.title: General Medical Council (Professional Conduct Committee) Rules

key_facts: Dr Phillips was acquitted at Crown Court on eight indecent assault counts after a severed trial; twenty-four related counts were stayed as an abuse of process.
The GMC referred twenty-five non-acquittal complaints to the Professional Conduct Committee, later adding five acquittal cases under Rule 11(2) after complainants' solicitors wrote in November 2003.
The doctor sought judicial review to prevent GMC inquiry into the five acquittal cases, arguing screening-out, unfair procedure, and abuse of process.
The court held criminal acquittal does not bar GMC misconduct proceedings where professional standards differ from criminal issues.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of the GMC's decision to refer five acquittal-related complaints to the Professional Conduct Committee.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed in respect of the five acquittal cases; agreed split hearing on abuse of process to precede substantive misconduct inquiry; claimant ordered to pay 60% of GMC costs.
enrichment.ratio: Acquittal on criminal charges does not prevent GMC consideration of serious professional misconduct, and Rule 11(2) may permit later inclusion of similar misconduct allegations after PCC referral where fresh grounds are adduced; pre-emptive judicial review to stop the PCC should be sparingly exercised and procedural fairness can be secured at the disciplinary hearing itself.
legal_issues: Whether acquittal bars GMC misconduct proceedings
Whether the five acquittal cases were validly added under Rule 11(2)
What 'later' means where the GMC already held complainant statements
Whether the doctor was denied a fair opportunity to respond before referral
linked_authorities: R (Redgrave) v Commissioner of the Metropolis [2003] 1 WLR 1136
R v Belmarsh Magistrates' Court ex parte Watts [1999] 1 Cr App R 188
R v Director of Public Prosecutions ex parte Kebilene [2000] 2 AC 326

confidence.notes: Disposal on the five acquittal cases and Rule 11(2) ruling are clear. Merits of underlying misconduct and abuse arguments were deliberately left for the PCC.

notes: Slander per se ruling under section 2 Defamation Act 1952; business and honorary office limbs both left to the jury.

enrichment.short_title: Slander per se for adultery imputation in business and charity offices
key_facts: The claimant CEO sued in slander alleging the defendant accused him of adultery with young married Jewish women.
The defendant applied for judgment on the basis that no special damage was pleaded and the words were not slander actionable per se.
The claimant ran a worldwide IT business with many dealings in the orthodox Jewish community and held trustee offices at a Sephardi school and related charity.
By agreement the issue was sent to the jury regardless of the judge's ruling, following Alexander v Arts Council of Wales.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory application for judgment entered in favour of the defendant on the slander claim before trial.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; slander claims held capable of being actionable per se under section 2 both in business and in office; issue to be determined by the jury.
enrichment.ratio: Section 2 of the Defamation Act 1952 uses 'any office' without preserving the old distinction between offices of profit and honour; where a claimant's business and community context make adultery allegations capable of discrediting him professionally, and where charitable trustee offices carry removal powers for misconduct, a jury may properly find slander actionable without proof of special damage.
legal_issues: Whether adultery allegations are capable of disparaging the claimant in his business under section 2
Whether charitable trustee roles qualify as 'office' under section 2
Whether offices of honour still require proof of special damage after the 1952 Act
Whether community religious context is relevant to the objective likelihood of disparagement

linked_authorities: Alexander v Arts Council of Wales [2001] 1 WLR 184
Alexander v Jenkins [1892] 1 QB 797
Jones v Jones [1916] AC 481
Robinson v Ward (1958)

notes: Bichard-related Chief Constable suspension challenge; short statutory construction judgment with clear outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Home Secretary validly required suspension of Humberside Chief Constable
key_facts: Following the Bichard Inquiry report into failings linked to the Soham murders, the Home Secretary required Humberside Police Authority to suspend Chief Constable Westwood under section 42(1A).
The police authority and chief constable challenged the instruction, arguing public confidence meant confidence only within Humberside.
The Home Secretary accepted he had regard to public confidence nationally, not merely locally.
The suspension was an interim step pending possible retirement/resignation procedures under the statutory protocol.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of the lawfulness of the Home Secretary's section 42(1A) suspension requirement.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; suspension requirement held valid; police authority under a continuing legal duty to suspend; leave to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Section 42(1A) of the Police Act 1996 requires the Home Secretary to consider whether suspension is necessary for the maintenance of public confidence in the force in question, meaning confidence of the public at large rather than only within the police area; where the Bichard findings provided strong grounds, national default powers were lawfully exercised.
legal_issues: Whether 'public confidence' in section 42(1A) is local or national
Whether the Home Secretary validly exercised the suspension power after the Bichard report
Whether public opinion differs from public confidence for this purpose
Who may review or terminate a Secretary of State-directed suspension

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and validity ruling are concise and unambiguous. Court did not adjudicate the merits of the Bichard criticisms themselves.

notes: AG reference on death by dangerous driving; unduly lenient finding but discretionary non-intervention is clearly explained.

enrichment.short_title: Unduly lenient community order for death by dangerous driving
key_facts: A 19-year-old soldier was convicted after trial of causing death by dangerous driving when his skidding car on the A1 at about 80-85 mph in rain caused a following lorry to stop suddenly and Anthony Broadhead's Fiesta collided with it fatally.
He had consumed alcohol below the legal limit but above levels shown to impair driving, and had had minimal sleep after a night out.
He was sentenced to a 180-hour community punishment order and five-year disqualification.
The deceased's speed, lack of seat belt, tyre wear, and seating position may have contributed to the fatal outcome.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging an unduly lenient non-custodial sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Reference found substantiated in principle—a custodial term of about two years would have been appropriate at first instance—but the Court declined to interfere because of double jeopardy, partial completion of the community order, and the limited utility of a very short remaining sentence.
enrichment.ratio: Causing death by dangerous driving will normally require a custodial sentence to reflect gravity and deterrence under Cooksley, and youth or contributory factors in the deceased's driving are not exceptional mitigating circumstances; however, the Court may exercise discretion not to increase sentence on reference where double jeopardy and progress on an existing community order make intervention pointless.
legal_issues: Whether a community punishment order was unduly lenient for causing death by dangerous driving
Application of the Cooksley sentencing guidelines
Whether contributory conduct by the deceased amounted to exceptional mitigation
Whether the Court should intervene despite double jeopardy and partial completion of the community sentence
linked_authorities: R v Cooksley [2004] 1 Cr App R (S) 1

confidence.notes: Unduly lenient finding and discretionary non-intervention are both clearly explained. Contributory causation by the deceased was accepted but held non-exceptional.
